prompt.context: A large food and beverage consumer packaged goods company (CPG) is the client. They have a 40% market share in traditional CPG channels, like large format grocery. They have a 17% market share in food service. They hired us to help them grow that food service business.
prompt.question: How would you structure growing the client's food service business?

clarifying_info.q: What does the client's beverage portfolio consist of?
clarifying_info.a: The beverage portfolio consists of sodas, waters, juices, teas, health drinks, and new specialty bottled drinks — no alcoholic beverages.

clarifying_info.q: What does the client's food portfolio consist of?
clarifying_info.a: The food portfolio consists primarily of snack foods for throughout the day (breakfast, lunch, and later).

clarifying_info.q: Who are the client's main competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client has one major competitor in beverage but no major competitor in their foods portfolio. The main competitor is a major beverage company with no food portfolio.

clarifying_info.q: What segments make up the food service market?
clarifying_info.a: There are four primary segments: 1) cafeteria/workplace food service, 2) restaurants (fast food, slow fast food/alternative fast food, and other), 3) entertainment/theme park venues, and 4) miscellaneous. Restaurants is the largest segment at about 70% of the food service market.

clarifying_info.q: What sub-segments exist within the restaurant segment?
clarifying_info.a: Fast food (e.g., Wendy's, BK, McDonald's), slow fast food/alternative fast food (e.g., Chipotle, Au Bon Pain, Cosi, California Pizza Kitchen Express, Wolfgang Puck's), and miscellaneous (corner deli, mom and pop, etc.).

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive situation within the restaurant sub-segments?
clarifying_info.a: The fast food sub-segment is dominated by the client's main competitor, who has a 70% market share there. Slow fast food/alternative fast food is a smaller but growing segment — growing at 30% a year — driven by the trend of eating healthier.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have any unique capabilities vs. competitors?
clarifying_info.a: No unique capabilities per se, but the key differentiator is that the client has both a food and a beverage portfolio, whereas the main competitor only has beverages.

exhibits.title: 3 Cs Framework Outline
exhibits.shows: A structured framework diagram organized around three columns: Customers, Company, and Competitors, each with bullet-point sub-questions
exhibits.data: Customers: Who are the potential customers in the food service market? (Cafeteria/Workplace food service; Restaurants—fast food, slow fast food, other; Entertainment venues—movie theaters, theme parks; Other?). Company: What's in our portfolio? (Food portfolio; Beverage portfolio); Do we have any capabilities that are specific to us? Competitors: Who are our competitors?; What do we have that differentiates us from our competition?; Where are our competitors strong? Where are we stronger than them? (Mkt. shares?)

framework: Use the 3 Cs framework: Customers, Company, Competitors
Customers: Map all food service segments (cafeteria/workplace, restaurants, entertainment/theme parks, misc.) and size them; identify where the 17% overall share breaks down by segment
Company: Audit the full portfolio (beverages — sodas, waters, juices, teas, health drinks, specialty; foods — snack foods across dayparts); identify differentiating capabilities
Competitors: Identify main competitor (beverage-only); assess where competitor is dominant (fast food at 70% share) and where the field is open
Prioritize: Focus on the largest segment (restaurants, 70% of food service) and within it the sub-segments not dominated by the competitor
Use 4 Ps to generate specific growth tactics within the priority sub-segments

questions.prompt: Which segment of the food service market should the client prioritize and why?
questions.guidance: The candidate should recognize that restaurants represent ~70% of the food service market and are the most attractive target. Within restaurants, the client should avoid the fast food sub-segment where the competitor holds 70% share. Instead focus on slow fast food/alternative fast food (growing at 30% per year, riding healthier-eating trends) and the mom-and-pop/misc. sub-segment where share is not locked up.

questions.prompt: How specifically should the client grow market share in the priority sub-segments? Use the 4 Ps.
questions.guidance: Product: Consider specialty or tailor-made products and custom packaging for restaurant customers. Price: Competing purely on price could grow unit share but would hurt dollar-volume share and compress margins — generally not recommended. Placement/Distribution: Client already distributes to a majority of the market, so incremental gains here are limited. Promotion: Create partnerships and cross-promotion campaigns with specific chains (advertising, coupons, loyalty programs). Leverage unique differentiator: Client is the only player with both food AND beverage offerings, which allows bundled selling and one-stop distribution to restaurant customers — a structural advantage the main competitor cannot match.

questions.prompt: What are the pros and cons of creating specialty or custom products for restaurant customers?
questions.guidance: Pros: Builds deeper, stickier relationships with restaurant customers; differentiates from the beverage-only competitor who cannot offer matching customization across both food and beverage. Cons: Profit margins on custom products will be lower due to smaller production runs and increased complexity; unit share may grow but overall bottom-line impact could be negative if margins erode.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the ways the client could grow market share in the non-fast-food restaurant sub-segments?

categories.name: Product
ideas: Develop specialty or custom-sized packaging for restaurant formats
Create new product formulations tailored to restaurant menus (e.g., lower-sugar beverages for health-oriented chains)
Bundle food and beverage products into combined offerings that the beverage-only competitor cannot match
Develop daypart-specific snack products aligned with restaurant service periods

categories.name: Price
ideas: Volume-based pricing incentives for restaurant chains committing to larger contracts
Bundled pricing discounts when restaurant buys both food and beverage products
Avoid pure price cuts that would erode margin; focus on value-based pricing instead

categories.name: Promotion
ideas: Co-branded advertising campaigns with slow fast food chains
Coupons or loyalty programs tied to restaurant purchases
Sponsorship of health/wellness events consistent with slow fast food brand positioning
Digital cross-promotion via restaurant apps or loyalty platforms

categories.name: Placement / Distribution
ideas: Target slow fast food chains not yet in the client's distribution network
Expand into mom-and-pop delis and smaller independents through a dedicated sales force or distributor partnerships
Offer consolidated delivery (food + beverage in one shipment) as a convenience advantage over competitors

categories.name: Portfolio Leverage
ideas: Pitch a combined food-and-beverage contract to restaurant customers, locking out the beverage-only competitor
Create restaurant-exclusive SKUs that cannot be purchased in traditional retail channels to protect margin

recommendation: The client should focus its food service growth efforts on the restaurant segment, which represents approximately 70% of the food service market

Within restaurants, avoid the fast food sub-segment where the main competitor holds 70% share; instead target slow fast food/alternative fast food (growing at 30% per year) and the mom-and-pop/misc. sub-segment
The primary growth lever is leveraging the client's unique dual portfolio (food + beverage) to offer bundled, one-stop solutions that the beverage-only competitor cannot match
Secondary levers include cross-promotion partnerships with fast-growing slow fast food chains and selectively developing custom products where margins are protected
risks: Custom products reduce margins and may grow unit share without improving bottom-line profitability
If the competitor acquires or develops a food portfolio, the client's key differentiator disappears
Fast food segment could become more accessible if the competitor's exclusive arrangements weaken, but for now it remains unfavorable to contest
Slow fast food is growing rapidly but the segment is currently small in absolute terms
next_steps: Conduct detailed market share analysis by sub-segment to identify exactly where the 17% overall share sits and where the largest gaps are
Pilot a bundled food-and-beverage offer with one or two slow fast food chain partners
Model margin impact of any proposed custom product line before committing to development
Evaluate distribution coverage gaps in mom-and-pop sub-segment and assess cost of closing them
